c: Sunrise Smoothie Bar, a smoothie shop near a university campus
s: Sunrise Smoothie Bar has been open for a year. Sales are strong at lunch but slow in the evening, and a new national chain has just opened two blocks away. The owner has a promotion budget of $4,000 for the next two months and wants to bring in more students after 4 p.m.

The owner (judge) is considering a student loyalty app, social media influencer posts and a happy-hour discount. Each has costs and risks. The owner wants you to analyze the situation and recommend a plan with a way to measure results.
You have 7 minutes to explain the problem, compare the alternatives with pros and cons, and recommend a promotional plan.
f: Promotion budget: $4,000 for two months
Average ticket: $7.80; evening traffic averages 25 customers, compared with 110 at lunch
Loyalty app: $1,800 setup; influencer posts: $1,500 for three accounts; happy hour 25% off: estimated cost $1,100 in discounts
A student survey: 62% of students say price matters most; 38% mention convenience and taste
Competitor chain offers a free drink after 8 purchases
n: Defines the target market and what the survey says about it
Compares the three promotions on cost, reach and risk, using numbers
Recommends a mix that fits $4,000, such as a happy hour plus a low-cost loyalty program
Explains how the plan responds to the national chain
Sets goals, such as raising evening traffic from 25 to 40 customers
Names measures and a timeline for evaluating results
q: Why not just match the chain's free drink offer?
How will you know the influencer money was worth it?
What would you cut if sales did not improve after a month?

c: Atlas Pet Supply, an online store that sells premium dog treats
s: Atlas Pet Supply sells a popular bag of organic dog treats for $14.99. Costs have risen, and the company's margin on the treats has fallen from 45 percent to 33 percent. A competitor sells a similar bag for $12.49, and customer reviews say Atlas's treats are higher quality. The vice president of marketing is deciding whether to raise the price, hold it, or reduce the package size.
The vice president (judge) wants you to analyze pricing options, including how customers may respond, and recommend a price strategy.
You have 7 minutes to explain the pricing factors, compare the alternatives with pros and cons, and recommend a decision.
f: Current price: $14.99; unit cost now about $10.04
Competitor price: $12.49 for a similar bag
Sales: 8,000 bags a month
Test data: at $15.99, expected sales fall about 12%; at $16.99, about 25%
Customer reviews: 4.7 stars versus 4.2 for the competitor
n: Explains pricing factors: cost, competition, demand and perceived value
Calculates profit at each price (about $39,600 now; about $41,900 at $15.99; about $41,700 at $16.99 with fewer sales)
Compares raising the price, holding the price, and shrinking the package, with pros and cons
Considers how quality and reviews support a premium price
Recommends a specific price and a test plan
Addresses the risk of customers switching to the competitor
q: Why not just match the competitor's price?
How would customers react to a smaller package at the same price?
What would you watch in the first month after changing the price?

c: Trailhead Bikes, a bike manufacturer planning a new electric commuter bike
s: Trailhead Bikes wants to launch an electric commuter bike priced at $1,600. Before spending $400,000 to start production, the product manager wants evidence that enough people will buy it. The company has a sales database, a customer email list of 22,000 people and a small research budget of $12,000.
The product manager (judge) wants you to propose how to gather and use marketing information to decide whether to go ahead, adjust the product or stop.
You have 7 minutes to present your research plan, compare the research methods, and describe how the information will guide the decision.
f: Research budget: $12,000; production start-up cost: $400,000
Customer email list: 22,000 people; past survey response rate about 6%
Online panel survey: $6,500 for 400 respondents; focus groups: $5,000 for two sessions; sales data analysis: no added cost
Two competitors sell e-bikes at $1,400 and $1,900
Break-even: 780 bikes at a $510 margin per bike
n: Distinguishes primary data from secondary data and gives examples of each
Compares surveys, focus groups and sales data with costs and limits
Explains sampling and why a response from 6% of the list may be biased
Proposes questions that test price, features and intent to buy
Recommends a plan within $12,000 and a decision rule, such as pre-order interest
Explains how results would change the product or price
q: How would you know the survey answers reflect real buyers?
What result would make you recommend stopping?
Why not use only our own sales data?

c: Evergreen Home Candles, a small company that makes handmade soy candles
s: Evergreen Home Candles sells mostly through its website and local craft fairs. A regional home décor chain has offered to stock its candles in 35 stores, but the chain would pay only 55 percent of the retail price. Another option is a popular online marketplace that takes a 15 percent fee. The owner worries about capacity and brand image.
The owner (judge) wants to know which sales channel to focus on over the next year: the home décor chain, the marketplace, expanding direct sales, or a combination.
You have 7 minutes to compare the channels, explain the trade-offs and recommend a plan.
f: Retail price per candle: $22; cost to make: $7.50
Chain order: 6,000 candles a year at 55% of retail ($12.10 each)
Marketplace: 15% fee plus shipping; estimated 3,500 candles a year
Direct sales: 4,200 candles a year at full price; growth expected at 10%
Production capacity: 12,000 candles a year
n: Explains the role of channels and intermediaries in reaching customers
Calculates the margin per candle in each channel ($4.60 chain, $11.20 marketplace before shipping, $14.50 direct)
Compares the options with pros and cons for volume, margin and brand image
Considers capacity limits
Recommends a mix and sets targets for the first year
Mentions how to track which channel performs best
q: Is a lower margin worth the volume from the chain?
What happens to our brand if our candles are in 35 stores?
What if we cannot make enough candles?

c: Brightside Solar, a company that installs rooftop solar panels for homes
s: Ms. Reed owns a house and is interested in solar panels but is unsure about the cost, the payback time and whether the roof is suitable. Her electric bill averages $165 a month. A typical system for her home costs $18,000 before a 30 percent tax credit and would offset about 80 percent of her bill.

You are the sales representative. Your job is to build rapport, identify her needs, present the benefits honestly, handle her concerns about cost and her roof's age, and ask for her decision. Financing is available at 5.9 percent for 15 years.
The judge will play Ms. Reed. You have 7 minutes to conduct the sales conversation.
f: Average electric bill: $165 a month ($1,980 a year)
System price: $18,000; tax credit 30% ($5,400); net $12,600
Estimated savings: about $1,580 a year (80% of the bill)
Roof: 12 years old with an expected life of 25 years
Financing option: 15 years at 5.9% with no money down
n: Opens with rapport and needs-based questions about her bill, goals and concerns
Explains features as benefits, using her numbers: net cost $12,600 and about 8-year payback
Responds honestly to the roof concern and offers a roof inspection
Handles the price objection with the tax credit and financing choice
Uses a trial close and asks for a next step, such as a site assessment
Follows up and keeps the relationship after the sale
q: That is a lot of money. How do I know I will really save?
My roof is already 12 years old. Is that a problem?
What happens if I sell the house in five years?
